cards.title: Build ecommerce landing pages with static site generation for crawler access
cards.summary: Use static site generation instead of client-side rendering so Google and AI crawlers receive fully rendered HTML immediately.
cards.use_when: Choosing the technical build for a new category landing page, local service page, or content hub that must rank and be quotable by AI answer engines.
steps: Decide up front that the page will ship as pre-rendered HTML, not a JavaScript-rendered shell that populates content after load. Crawlers that don't execute JavaScript (and AI answer-engine crawlers especially) only see what's in the initial response.
Scaffold the site or page in a static site generator so every product, category, and content URL exists as complete HTML at build time.
Keep dynamic personalization or interactive widgets as progressive enhancements layered on top, not as the source of the core text a shopper or bot needs.
After deploy, fetch a sample URL and view the raw response (view-source or curl) to confirm headings, body copy, and internal links are present without JavaScript execution.
caveats: Static generation is the source's stated requirement for crawler-accessible content; it is not a universal rule — some platforms render server-side rather than statically and can achieve the same result.
Verify current tooling behavior before committing, since static frameworks and crawler capabilities change.

cards.title: Create a Claude.md SOP file before building store pages
cards.summary: A core instruction markdown file trains the AI coding agent on your SOPs, design references, and formatting rules before it scaffolds anything.
cards.use_when: Setting up an AI coding assistant to generate consistent store pages, templates, or content across a full catalog or site build.
steps: Write a Claude.md (or equivalent project instruction) file before prompting for page builds. Include: the site's purpose, target customer, tone rules, heading hierarchy, image sizing, alt-text conventions, internal linking rules, and any brand do/don'ts.
Attach or reference design examples — the source suggests Dribbble screenshots — plus existing pages you consider canonical, so the agent matches your layout rather than inventing one.
State formatting rules explicitly (e.g., how product names, prices, and CTA buttons are written) so output is consistent across dozens of pages.
Re-run or refresh the instruction file whenever you change templates or brand direction, so old rules don't leak into new pages.
caveats: The quality of generated pages is bounded by the specificity of your SOP file; vague instructions produce generic output.
Treat this as a starting scaffold you review, not an unreviewed publish pipeline.

cards.title: Filter keywords by difficulty and volume for product and service pages
cards.summary: Use keyword difficulty under 30 and search volume over 100 as a starting filter when picking target keywords.
cards.use_when: Deciding which keywords to build product pages, category pages, or buying-guide content around, especially for a new or low-authority store.
steps: Pull a candidate keyword list from a tool like SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool around your product categories and services.
Apply the source's starting filter: difficulty under 30 and search volume over 100. This surfaces terms a smaller site can realistically rank for rather than head terms dominated by major retailers.

Split the filtered list by intent: informational queries (how-to, comparison, care guides) for content pages; commercial intent — including service-plus-city combinations like 'service + city' — for pages that convert.
Map each surviving keyword to a specific page type (product page, category page, guide, local page) so two pages don't compete for the same term.
Recheck difficulty and volume in the current tool data before committing, since these thresholds are the source's heuristic, not a guaranteed ranking formula.
caveats: Difficulty under 30 and volume over 100 are source-specific heuristics, not established benchmarks; adjust for your niche and authority.
Volume thresholds may exclude valuable long-tail or high-intent terms with low but highly qualified traffic.

cards.title: Reverse-engineer top competitor content to build a superior page
cards.summary: Analyze top-ranking competitor pages to extract winning structures, word counts, and heading distributions, then synthesize a stronger draft.
cards.use_when: Planning the structure of a buying guide, category page, or service page where you need to match what already ranks before differentiating.
steps: For each target keyword, identify the pages currently ranking on page one and pull their content.
Prompt the AI agent (or analyze manually) to calculate the average word count and the heading distribution across those top pages — how many H2s, what each covers, in what order.
Identify what the winning formula consistently covers, then write a draft that covers all of it plus gaps competitors missed (specs, comparisons, sizing, care, FAQs).
Match or exceed the observed word count and heading depth only where it adds real information — padding to hit a number is not the goal.
Revisit quarterly, since ranking structures shift as competitors update.
caveats: Mimicking a competitor's word count doesn't guarantee ranking; usefulness and intent match still matter.
Average word counts from a small sample can mislead — check that top results are genuinely comparable to your page type.

cards.title: Train the AI on your voice and brand stories to avoid generic AI content
cards.summary: Feed the AI your personal voice, brand stories, and humor so generated content reads as authored rather than templated.
cards.use_when: Producing product descriptions, buying guides, or brand content at scale where generic output would hurt conversion and trust.
steps: Collect samples of your best existing copy: emails, product stories, founder notes, replies that customers responded well to.
Extract and document concrete voice rules in your instruction file: sentence length, formality, signature phrases, what humor is and isn't acceptable, words you avoid.
Include real brand stories and specifics — origin, materials, why you stock what you stock — so the content has substance competitors can't copy.
Generate drafts, then edit for the rules rather than accepting the first pass; the source specifically flags 'AI slop' as a risk.
Spot-check new pages against a voice checklist before publishing.
caveats: AI-generated content still needs human review; the source treats voice training as the mitigation, not a replacement for editing.
Humor and personality that work in one category may misfire in another — test against your audience.

cards.title: Use the zipper method to combine services with locations for local pages
cards.summary: Pair each service offering with each target municipality to harvest local-intent searches without writing unique copy from scratch.
cards.use_when: Building local landing pages for a store that serves multiple cities or regions, or a service area business attached to a physical store.
steps: List your core service or product offerings in one column and your target cities/towns in another.
Generate a page for each meaningful service-plus-city combination that has real search demand, not every possible permutation.
For each page, include genuinely local detail — delivery/coverage area, local examples, references to the community — so pages aren't thin duplicates that risk being filtered.
Use your Claude.md SOP and voice rules so all zipped pages stay on-brand and consistent.
Prioritize combinations with measurable local search volume and filter out ones where you'd be duplicating content without adding local value.
caveats: Mass-generated location pages with no unique local content risk being treated as thin or duplicate; the source's method assumes you add local substance.
Verify local search demand per combination rather than generating the full matrix blindly.

cards.title: Loop Lighthouse reports back into Claude Code until scores reach 100
cards.summary: Run Google Lighthouse in Chrome DevTools, paste the performance/SEO errors into Claude Code, and have the agent rewrite code until the audit passes.
cards.use_when: Fixing slow or technically flawed product, category, or landing pages that underperform on Core Web Vitals and technical SEO.
steps: Run a Google Lighthouse audit on the page in Chrome DevTools across all four categories: performance, SEO, accessibility, and best practices.
Copy the full error report and paste it into Claude Code along with the page source.
Command the agent to fix the specific flagged issues (unused scripts, large images, missing meta, contrast failures) and iterate until the scores hit 100.
Re-run the audit after each change to confirm fixes actually resolved the flagged items rather than shifting the problem.
As an ongoing habit, wire Lighthouse checks into your build or deploy step so regressions are caught before they ship.
caveats: 100/100 across all four Lighthouse categories is the source's target and can be difficult to sustain on content-heavy pages; treat it as a direction, not a guarantee of rankings.
Lighthouse is a lab audit — real-user field metrics may differ.
Verify current Lighthouse and DevTools interface before following exact steps, since they change.

cards.title: Deploy via GitHub and Vercel, then submit sitemaps to search consoles
cards.summary: Push the built site to GitHub, deploy via Vercel, then submit XML sitemaps to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
cards.use_when: Taking a new or rebuilt storefront or landing page live and making sure search engines and AI crawlers can find it.
steps: Push the repository to GitHub so the build is version-controlled and deployable.
Deploy via Vercel (or your chosen host) to get the static site published with fast global delivery.
Generate an XML sitemap covering all product, category, and content URLs.
Submit the sitemap to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools so both index the new pages.
After submission, monitor indexing status and coverage errors, and confirm pages that should rank are actually being crawled.
caveats: Hosting and console interfaces change; verify current steps in Vercel, Search Console, and Bing Webmaster Tools before executing.
Submission doesn't guarantee indexing — thin or duplicate pages may be excluded.

cards.title: Prioritize AEO alongside traditional SEO for ecommerce content
cards.summary: Optimize content so it's both crawlable by search engines and structured to be quoted by AI answer engines.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in answer-engine optimization for product FAQs, buying guides, or comparison content.
steps: Recognize the shift: shoppers increasingly get answers from AI engines rather than clicking blue links, so content must be extractable as a direct answer.
Write clear, self-contained answers to real customer questions (sizing, materials, compatibility, shipping) near the top of relevant pages so they can be lifted cleanly.
Keep pages statically rendered so AI crawlers that don't run JavaScript can read them (see the SSG card).
Use consistent heading structure and concise factual statements rather than buried prose, so both Google and answer engines can parse your content.
Track whether your content appears in AI-generated answers and adjust — the source frames AEO as the emerging frontier, so treat tactics as evolving.
caveats: AEO is a stated priority of the source, not a proven equal to traditional SEO; treat the specific tactics as emerging practice.
AI answer engines and their crawl behavior change frequently — verify current behavior before relying on any single tactic.

cards.title: Keep SEO builds inside the right tool and platform boundaries
cards.summary: Separate SEO/site-generation work from paid ads, tracking, and ecommerce platform backend configuration.
cards.use_when: Scoping an SEO project and deciding which work belongs in the SEO workflow versus your ad, analytics, or Shopify backend workflows.
steps: Keep paid ad campaign strategy and Meta Ads tracking in your advertising/measurement workflow — don't mix ad tracking setup into an SEO build.
Handle Shopify backend settings (inventory, taxes, shipping) in the platform's own configuration process, not as SEO tasks.
Keep SEO work focused on: site generation, keyword research, competitor analysis, content scaling, service-page architecture, technical SEO, and deployment.
When a task spans areas (e.g., a new landing page needs both SEO copy and an ad destination), define which team or workflow owns each part to avoid duplicated or conflicting execution.
caveats: This scoping is the source's division of labor, not a hard industry rule; adapt to your team.
Overlapping concerns (like tracking on a landing page) may reasonably involve both workflows — coordinate rather than exclude entirely.

input.text:
16-AEO / answer engine optimization Goes here. A comprehensive masterclass on utilizing Claude Code and SEMrush to execute an end-to-end SEO and AI search strategy. Covers generating static sites via Claude Code, filtering low-difficulty keywords, scraping competitor formulas, incorporating personal voice/humor into AI-generated content, setting up automated SEO skills, optimizing Lighthouse performance scores (technical SEO), and deploying via GitHub and Vercel. Not here. • Paid ad campaign strategies or Meta Ads tracking -> 06-MEA • Shopify backend configurations (inventory, taxes, shipping) -> 05-SET

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a cutting-edge approach to modern SEO and AI search optimization by leveraging AI coding assistants (Claude Code) to automate technical setup, content writing, and site performance optimization at scale. modules: [AEO] topics: [Claude Code, static site generation, keyword research, SEO automation, technical SEO, Lighthouse optimization, content scaling] tier: 3 scope_hint: comprehensive

Topics. site generation / using Claude Code and a foundational Claude.md file to rapidly build static-site-generation (SSG) web apps optimized for crawler indexing; keyword research / utilizing SEMrush Keyword Magic Tool to find keywords with a difficulty under 30 and search volume over 100, focusing on informational queries and service-city commercial intent; competitor analysis / analyzing top-ranking competitor pages to extract winning content structures, word counts, and heading distributions; content scaling / training Claude on personal voice, brand stories, and humor (avoiding AI slop) and prompting it to reverse-engineer top competitors; service page architecture / implementing the "zipper" method to combine service offerings with municipal locations to capture local intent; technical SEO / using Google Lighthouse performance reports to identify and feed performance issues back into Claude Code until the site hits 100/100 scores across SEO, accessibility, best practices, and performance; deployment / pushing repositories to GitHub and deploying instantly via Vercel before submitting XML sitemaps to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.

Look for. * Static Site Generation (SSG): The technical requirement to build sites using static site generation rather than client-side rendering, ensuring Google and AI crawler bots can instantly access and index fully rendered HTML without waiting for JavaScript execution.

The Claude.md SOP File: Utilizing a core instruction markdown file (Claude.md) to train the AI coding agent on standard operating procedures, design references (via Dribbble screenshots), and formatting rules before scaffolding the site.

Competitor Content Reverse Engineering: Prompting Claude to analyze the top-ranking search results for a target keyword, calculate average word counts and heading structures, and synthesize a superior draft based on the winning formula.

Lighthouse Score Remediation: The automated loop of running a Google Lighthouse audit in Chrome Developer Tools, copying the performance/SEO error report, pasting it directly into Claude Code, and commanding the AI to rewrite the code until hitting a 100% score.

Skip. Promotional pitches for Pexels API setups, Namecheap domain purchases, and the creator's paid agency/community programs.

Scope mix. 10% baseline (traditional SEO metrics), 90% growth (AI-driven development, Claude Code automation, and modern tech stack deployment). Volume. ~450 words.
